title: Company background:
caseText:
Vardhan Precision Forgings Ltd. (VPFL) manufactures specialized steel components for commercial vehicles and railways. Over the last three years, annual revenue grew steadily by 14% to reach ₹620 crore, supported by consistent operating cash flows and a stable EBITDA margin of 16%. VPFL currently maintains low leverage, with a Debt-to-EBITDA ratio of 1.6x and an Interest Coverage Ratio (ICR) of 4.2x.

VPFL is requesting a 6-year term loan of ₹120 crore to set up an automated forging line in Pune, pledging the new plant and machinery as primary collateral alongside a 25% promoter equity contribution. While domestic railway demand remains strong, a single European automotive client accounts for 35% of total revenue. Recently, VPFL’s illustrative stock price fell by 18% after market analysts flagged rising energy costs in Europe; however, stock-price performance is contextual market evidence and not a substitute for fundamental credit analysis. Additionally, alloy steel input prices have become volatile, and the European client is currently renegotiating its three-year supply contract, requesting a 60-day extension in credit terms without a fixed minimum off-take guarantee.

questions.question: Based on the credit profile and business outlook provided, what is the most prudent lending decision for the bank regarding VPFL’s ₹120 crore loan request?

options.text: Sanction the full ₹120 crore loan with standard covenants, as the company’s strong historical operating cash flows and 25% equity contribution provide adequate cushion against client concentration.
Reject the loan proposal immediately, because the 18% decline in the company's stock price and European headwinds indicate an imminent deterioration in core solvency.
Sanction the loan subject to specific risk-mitigating conditions, including raw material price pass-through verification and tighter working capital covenants to manage extended receivables.
Defer the loan decision until the company replaces its European client with domestic railway contracts to eliminate foreign revenue exposure completely.

questions.question: Which factor represents the most material threat to VPFL’s debt service coverage over the tenure of the proposed term loan?

options.text: The existing Debt-to-EBITDA ratio of 1.6x, which leaves no headroom for capital expenditure borrowing.
Potential compression in operating cash flows from simultaneous raw material cost volatility and elongated receivable cycles from its largest customer.
The recent 18% correction in the company’s equity market valuation, which directly reduces the liquidation value of the proposed plant and machinery collateral.
The dependence on the domestic railway sector, which typically offers lower operating margins than export markets.

questions.question: Why does the 18% drop in VPFL’s illustrative stock price have limited standalone weight in determining whether the bank should reject the credit facility?

options.text: Equity market movements often reflect short-term investor sentiment regarding growth expectations, whereas credit appraisal focuses on downside cash-flow stability and debt servicing ability.
Stock prices only affect a company's ability to raise working capital from commercial banks, having no bearing on long-term project finance loans.
The Reserve Bank of India prohibits commercial banks from reviewing capital market indicators when appraising secured manufacturing term loans.
A declining stock price improves the borrower's creditworthiness because management becomes less likely to distribute cash flows as dividends to shareholders.

questions.question: Assume that before disbursement, the European client cancels its contract entirely, and VPFL decides to fund the entire ₹120 crore expansion through debt by withdrawing its 25% promoter equity contribution. How should the bank revise its stance?

options.text: Proceed with the sanction by increasing the interest rate by 150 basis points to compensate for the higher leverage and loss of revenue visibility.
Defer or reject the current proposal, as the simultaneous loss of 35% revenue visibility and removal of promoter skin-in-the-game fundamentally alters project viability and leverage.
Sanction the full amount provided the promoters pledge their unencumbered listed shares to cover the 25% equity shortfall.
Approve 65% of the loan amount immediately without requiring promoter equity, scaling the debt down proportionally to the remaining domestic revenue share.

title: Company background:
caseText:
QuantEdge Broking & Algo-Tech Ltd. is a listed fintech firm providing low-latency algorithmic execution platforms to retail discount brokers and proprietary trading desks. Driven by a surge in derivatives trading volumes, its revenue doubled over two years to ₹280 crore, with a healthy EBITDA margin of 28% and minimal long-term debt of ₹15 crore. QuantEdge seeks an ₹85 crore 4-year facility to upgrade its co-location server infrastructure and meet increased working capital margin requirements at clearing corporations.

As security, the company offers a charge on its software intellectual property (IP) and office furniture, plus a personal guarantee from the founders. However, 65% of QuantEdge’s revenue comes from just three retail discount brokerages. Furthermore, the market regulator has released a consultation paper proposing stricter position limits and higher lot sizes on index options to curb speculative retail trading. QuantEdge’s illustrative stock valuation trades at a high price-to-earnings multiple, though equity optimism does not mitigate cash-flow volatility. Operating cash flows fluctuate sharply from quarter to quarter depending on market turnover, and one major brokerage client is already building an in-house execution engine.

questions.question: What is the primary credit weakness in QuantEdge’s proposal that prevents the bank from treating its 28% EBITDA margin and low debt as sufficient grounds for an unconditional sanction?

options.text: The high price-to-earnings multiple in the stock market, which indicates that the company’s financial statements are likely overstated.
The mismatch between a 4-year loan tenure and server hardware, which normally has a productive lifespan exceeding 15 years.
The company’s refusal to utilize equity capital markets for working capital despite trading at a favorable valuation.
High earnings sensitivity to regulatory tightening in derivatives volumes, compounded by severe customer concentration and intangible, hard-to-liquidate collateral.

questions.question: How should the credit committee evaluate the collateral package offered by QuantEdge (software IP, office furniture, and founder personal guarantees)?

options.text: As inadequate standalone credit protection, because software IP rapidly loses value if regulatory shifts or client attrition impair the underlying business model.
As robust primary security, since proprietary trading algorithms generate high margins and can be easily auctioned to competing banks in the event of default.
As sufficient to waive cash-flow covenants, provided the founders’ personal net worth is currently tied to their shareholding in QuantEdge.
As unacceptable under banking norms, because commercial banks are only permitted to lend against immovable industrial land and physical inventory.

questions.question: Considering the pending regulatory changes and client insourcing risk, what is the most defensible lending decision for the bank?

options.text: Sanction the full ₹85 crore unconditionally to capture a high-growth fintech relationship before competing banks offer lower interest rates.
Sanction a reduced loan amount focused strictly on verifiable hardware capex, backed by a Debt Service Reserve Account (DSRA), cash-sweep covenants, and tangible cash margin collateral.
Reject the proposal solely because service-sector companies with less than ₹500 crore in revenue lack the asset base required for corporate debt.
Defer the decision for three years until the equity market enters a prolonged bear phase to observe how the company performs under stress.

questions.question: Suppose the market regulator implements the stricter derivatives norms immediately, causing QuantEdge’s monthly trading turnover to drop by 45%, while its largest client (accounting for 30% of revenue) terminates its contract upon completing its in-house platform. What should the bank do?

options.text: Sanction the ₹85 crore facility immediately, as the company will urgently need liquidity to survive the revenue downturn and develop new products.
Reject the term loan request, as the structural erosion of its core revenue stream and client base compromises primary repayment capacity beyond what covenants can mitigate.
Approve the loan on the condition that QuantEdge pledges its treasury stock as collateral to cover the 45% revenue shortfall.
Convert the ₹85 crore request into an unsecured 10-year project loan to give the company lower monthly repayment obligations during the industry transition.

title: Company background:
caseText:
Dakshin-Path Tollways & Infra Corp. (DPTIC) is an EPC and build-operate-transfer (BOT) road developer with annual revenues of ₹1,450 crore. While its order book stands at a healthy ₹4,200 crore, consolidated debt has risen to ₹2,900 crore, pulling its Interest Coverage Ratio down to 1.25x. DPTIC is requesting a ₹300 crore term loan for equipment purchases and mobilization advances for a newly awarded highway project.

Despite steady construction margins of 13%, operating cash flows have been negative for two consecutive years. Nearly ₹680 crore of DPTIC’s net worth is locked as equity investments and unsecured loans in three operational toll-road subsidiaries (SPVs) where commercial traffic has fallen 30% short of initial projections due to competing state highways. Furthermore, ₹450 crore in receivables is tied up in prolonged arbitration claims with state nodal agencies. The company’s promoters have already pledged 72% of their shareholding to existing lenders. DPTIC offers a subservient charge on current assets and a corporate guarantee from one of its underperforming toll SPVs as security for the ₹300 crore loan.

questions.question: What is the most appropriate decision for the bank regarding DPTIC’s ₹300 crore loan application?

options.text: Sanction the loan in full, as the ₹4,200 crore order book guarantees sufficient future revenue to resolve current liquidity mismatches.
Approve ₹150 crore immediately against the ₹450 crore arbitration claims, treating disputed receivables as cash equivalents.
Sanction the loan subject to the promoters pledging the remaining 28% of their unencumbered equity shares as primary collateral.

Reject the proposal, as the combination of chronically negative operating cash flows, low interest coverage (1.25x), trapped capital in distressed SPVs, and weak security presents unacceptable credit risk.

questions.question: In assessing DPTIC’s balance sheet and cash flows, what is the core analytical flaw in relying on its reported net worth and ₹450 crore receivable balance to justify additional lending?

options.text: Accounting net worth and book receivables do not pay interest; when capital is illiquid in underperforming SPVs and disputed claims, real debt-servicing liquidity is severely overstated.
Construction companies are required to write off all state nodal agency receivables within 90 days, making the reported balance legally invalid.
A high order book automatically reduces a company's net worth by increasing its future tax liabilities.
Subservient charges on current assets give the new lender priority over existing consortium banks in liquidating the arbitration claims.

questions.question: Why does the corporate guarantee from the operational toll SPV fail to provide meaningful credit enhancement for the proposed ₹300 crore facility?

options.text: Corporate guarantees from subsidiary companies are legally unenforceable under Indian banking and contract law.
Toll Road SPVs collect revenue in cash, which cannot be routed through commercial bank escrow accounts for debt repayment.
An SPV experiencing a 30% traffic shortfall is already struggling to service its own project-level debt, offering negligible residual cash flow to support the parent company's obligations.
The SPV’s guarantee would only become valid after the parent company completes 100% of its ₹4,200 crore order book.

questions.question: Assume DPTIC enters a binding agreement with an Infrastructure Investment Trust (InvIT) to sell two of its toll SPVs for ₹950 crore in cash, committed solely to retiring existing debt, and requests the bank to fund only a ₹100 crore ring-fenced project facility backed by an escrow on central government annuity payments. How should the bank respond?

options.text: Maintain the outright rejection, because any company that has experienced negative operating cash flows in the past cannot be lent to for five years.

Defer the decision until the ₹950 crore InvIT sale closes and debt reduction is verified, with a view to sanctioning the ring-fenced ₹100 crore facility once leverage and cash-flow ring-fencing are established.
Sanction the original ₹300 crore loan immediately without waiting for the InvIT transaction to close, relying on the press announcement of the sale.
Reject the ₹100 crore ring-fenced structure because annuity payments from central agencies carry higher traffic risk than state toll roads.

title: Company background:
caseText:
ArogyaSynth API Pharmaceuticals Ltd. manufactures Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs) for cardiovascular and anti-diabetic drugs, generating ₹880 crore in annual revenue. Two years ago, its EBITDA margin dipped from 20% to 12% due to sudden price spikes in imported chemical Key Starting Materials (KSMs) and higher freight costs. Following backward integration and renegotiated annual supply contracts, margins recovered to 17.5% over the last two quarters. Leverage remains moderate with a Debt-to-EBITDA ratio of 2.3x and an Interest Coverage Ratio of 3.1x.

ArogyaSynth seeks a ₹160 crore 5-year term loan to commission a backward-integrated fermentation unit that qualifies under the government’s Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme, aiming to reduce imported KSM dependence from 65% to 25%. The company offers a first pari-passu charge on fixed assets (asset coverage ratio of 1.8x). However, the US Food and Drug Administration (USFDA) recently concluded a routine inspection at ArogyaSynth’s flagship plant—which contributes 40% of revenue—and issued three procedural observations regarding laboratory data logging. Management has submitted corrective actions, and final regulatory clearance is expected within 60 days.

questions.question: What is the most commercially and financially sound course of action for the bank regarding ArogyaSynth’s ₹160 crore loan request?

options.text: Sanction and disburse the ₹160 crore loan immediately without conditions, because backward integration under the PLI scheme eliminates all operational and regulatory risks.

Defer final disbursement (or make sanction contingent) until the USFDA inspection observations are satisfactorily resolved, as an adverse escalation at a plant generating 40% of revenue could severely impair repayment capacity.
Reject the proposal permanently, because the historical margin drop from 20% to 12% proves that the pharmaceutical API sector is structurally unprofitable.
Sanction the loan immediately by taking a second charge on imported KSM inventory instead of fixed assets to bypass regulatory uncertainty.

questions.question: How should the credit analyst interpret the decline in ArogyaSynth’s EBITDA margin to 12% two years ago and its subsequent recovery to 17.5%?

options.text: It reflects temporary input cost and supply-chain pressure that management is actively addressing through backward integration, rather than permanent business deterioration.
It proves that the company manipulates its accounting depreciation schedules every two years to artificially boost reported margins prior to applying for bank loans.
It indicates that the company’s cardiovascular and anti-diabetic API portfolio has become medically obsolete and faces permanent demand destruction.
It demonstrates that revenue growth in the pharmaceutical industry always causes operating margins to contract due to regulatory compliance costs.

questions.question: Why is the resolution of the USFDA observations at the flagship facility critical to the bank’s credit appraisal, even though the proposed ₹160 crore loan is for a new domestic fermentation unit?

options.text: Under Indian banking regulations, a company with any pending foreign regulatory observation is legally barred from operating domestic bank accounts.
During the construction and ramp-up phase of the new unit, the company’s existing operating cash flows—heavily reliant on the flagship plant—must service the interest and existing debt obligations.
The USFDA holds the legal authority to seize the new domestic fermentation equipment if procedural observations at another plant are not resolved within 30 days.
The government’s PLI scheme only reimburses capital expenditure for companies that export 100% of their production to the United States.

questions.question: Suppose ArogyaSynth receives an Establishment Inspection Report (EIR) clearing the USFDA observations within 45 days, and subsequently requests loan disbursement. Which covenant structure is most appropriate for sanctioning the ₹160 crore facility?

options.text: Sanction the loan with no financial covenants, since regulatory clearance guarantees that the company will maintain a 20% EBITDA margin indefinitely.
Sanction the loan on the condition that ArogyaSynth halts all exports to regulated markets to avoid future inspection costs.
Sanction only ₹40 crore and require the company to fund the remaining ₹120 crore through short-term 90-day commercial paper rollovers.

Sanction the loan subject to project completion milestones, a cap on total Debt-to-EBITDA at 2.75x, mandatory hedging on unhedged foreign currency exposure, and routing of project cash flows through an escrow/trust and retention account.
